justification:
This round's job was to confirm the writer's three AdSense-driven edits introduced no new technical error, with the tree/parent claim getting independent verification since it touches a factual claim about the git object model. All three check out.

1) The golden-rule sentence. Round 1's wording — 'a rebase does not edit a commit, it writes a new one with the same tree and a different parent' — was already factually wrong for this article's own demonstrated scenario: the 'What git rebase writes instead' section (unchanged this round) explicitly shows and states that annotate~1 and annotate-for-rebase~1 have unequal trees ('Their full trees are not equal either, because annotate-for-rebase~1's tree also carries "Apr: The Fifth Season"... a commit's identity does not depend only on its tree. It also hashes its parent, and the parents differ'). So round 1's golden-rule sentence directly contradicted the demonstration two sections earlier in the same article — a genuine internal inconsistency, correctly flagged for this round's fix even though round 1's technical reviewer did not catch it (the tree/parent distinction sat in prose the round-1 review's runCode-adjacent checks did not specifically re-derive). The round-2 wording — 'it writes a new one with a new tree as well as a new parent — replaying a commit onto a different base changes what it contains, not only where it sits — so the old and new versions are unrelated objects that happen to carry the same edit' — now says exactly what 'What git rebase writes instead' already showed. I verified the underlying git mechanics independently, both by reasoning through the object model and by reproducing it in a scratch repo outside the harness: git rebase replays each commit as a three-way merge of (old parent, new base, original commit), so the resulting tree equals the original only in the degenerate case where the new base's tree is byte-identical to the old parent's; whenever the new base carries content the old parent didn't (which is the entire reason to rebase onto it, and is exactly what 'Add April books' does relative to 'Add March books' in this article's scenario), the replayed commit's tree necessarily changes too, and its parent hash always changes because the parent object itself is different. My scratch-repo reproduction (base commit, divergent old-parent and new-base commits, a feature commit rebased across them) shows tree, parent and full commit hash all differing before vs. after, matching the article's own explicit demonstration that annotate-for-rebase~1's tree includes April's line while annotate~1's does not. The claim is genuinely true, not merely now self-consistent — round 1's version was the one in error, and round 2 fixes it correctly. The golden-rule paragraph's 'shown twice over' back-reference also holds up: the tip-level demonstration (before_tip vs. after_tip) and the individual-commit-level demonstration (annotate~1 vs. annotate-for-rebase~1, including the explicit tree-and-parent breakdown) are the two places within 'What git rebase writes instead' that this sentence is generalizing from, and both are consistent with the new wording.

2) The rev-parse code block. The new block computes `same=$(git rev-parse annotate~1)` and `rebased=$(git rev-parse annotate-for-rebase~1)`, then echoes `"same object: $([ "$same" = "$rebased" ] && echo yes || echo no)"`. This is the same yes/no pattern already used a few lines earlier in the same section for `before_tip`/`after_tip` (round 1 verified that pattern correct), and it is correct here too: round 1's independent reproduction already established that `annotate~1` and `annotate-for-rebase~1` hash to two different SHA-1s (ac26f6b… vs. e3d0a89…), so `[ "$same" = "$rebased" ]` is false, the `&&` branch is skipped, `|| echo no` fires, and the block prints exactly the claimed `same object: no`. I re-ran `node tools/run-code.mjs` twice from PowerShell and got PASS at blocks=22 executed=11 both times, identical to round 1, confirming this block's actual output matches the article's `text output` exactly under the pinned harness environment. I also grepped the whole file for any bare 7-40-character hex sequence and for any other `rev-parse` call: the only two `rev-parse` invocations left in the file are this pair and the pre-existing `before_tip`/`after_tip` pair a few lines above, both already captured into shell variables rather than echoed raw, and there is no raw commit hash printed anywhere else in the article. The writer did not miss a spot.

3) The --is-ancestor quote. I fetched the live git-merge-base documentation fresh this round (both a summarized fetch and a raw curl of the HTML, to see the exact source markup). The --is-ancestor entry reads, with its `<commit>` placeholder spans taken as plain text: 'Check if the first commit is an ancestor of the second commit, and exit with status 0 if true, or with status 1 if not. Errors are signaled by a non-zero status that is not 1.' Round 1's quote had silently shifted this into third-person/paraphrase mood ('checks'... 'exits'...), which is exactly the kind of unmarked tense change the round-2 fix targets; the new quote correctly restores the documentation's actual imperative mood ('Check'... One residual, pre-existing imprecision: both round 1 and round 2 drop the second occurrence of the word 'commit' ('the second' instead of 'the second commit'), and neither round renders the source's `<commit>` placeholder markup at all (a reasonable normalization for inline prose, but strictly speaking not letter-for-letter identical to the source).
